header.title: De Musica Librorum Quae Exstant: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Philodemus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg1595.tlg221.1st1K-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg1595.tlg221.1st1K-gr: Fr. 1 is supplemented by Kemke from Plato, Laws 669B, which the edition prints with it; the restorations follow that model. In fr. 3 (pap. 424) line 8 'χαιτοϲϲ' is unintelligible and left untranslated; several lines there are too damaged to render. Fr. 13B line 3 'ϲυνεπικοϲμθῖν' read as ϲυνεπικοϲμεῖν ('add as ornament'). Fr. 10 (IX 71) line 1 restored ἀνδρεῖα may be 'manly [things]'. In XI 80 fr. 12 the subject of 'admits' and 'wrote' is not named in the surviving text. Damon in fr. 9 is presumably the fifth-century Athenian music theorist.

The text is very fragmentary and heavily restored by the editor. In 18.6 'δειθυραμβικοὺϲ' is read as διθυραμβικοὺϲ. In 25.1 the numbering '20 διαθε' is probably a misprint for 26. In 27.14 Ptolemy and the piper Ismenias are as the editor restores them; κέλευϲμα is the rowers' time-call. In 28.5 'ἀκατ . . .' could not be construed.

Highly fragmentary text; many supplements are the editor's conjectures and are translated as marked. 1.28.35–37 quotes Homer, Odyssey 14.464–465. 1.30.34–36 quotes Pindar (fr. 109). 1.30.7–8: the words before the break are unclear in the papyrus. 1.31.51–52: Archilochus fragment. In 1.31.44 πρὸ〈ϲ〉 is an editorial correction. In 3.9.3 ἀ]νθρμπιν is evidently ἀνθρωπίνην, a scanning error, rendered 'human'. In 3.6.11 the restoration is doubtful.

Text is fragmentary throughout; many renderings rest on the editor's supplements. 3.20.8 ἐφόρων may be 'ephors' (Spartan magistrates) or 'overseers'. 3.21.1 θείας could also belong to a compound ending in -θεια. 3.13.12 ἔμθεά read as ἔνθεα ('inspired'). 3.27.15 μέ[νον] is uncertain and the sense of the line unclear. Editorial headings and Latin notes ('sequitur fortasse', 'pauca leguntur') are rendered in English.

The text is extremely fragmentary throughout; many lines give only isolated words. Lines with Latin editorial summaries ("pauca leguntur", "nimis exile fragmentum", "extremae modo uersuum litterae exstant") are translated as summaries of the legible words. "lepuntur" in 47.1 read as "leguntur"; "ὁμπλογῴην" in 49.2 read as "ὁμολογοίην"; "ἑκάϲ[οτ]τε" in 48.5 read as "ἑκάϲτοτε" (repeatedly, each time), here given as "from each" — the sense could also be "each time". In 41.15–17 the restoration μακρὰν ... ἀνάϲταϲιν is uncertain; "return"/"restoration" for ἀνάϲταϲιν is a guess. In 37.6–7 the bracketed μὴ makes the sense difficult.

Extremely fragmentary throughout; only connected sense is translated, gaps kept as '. . .'. Headings giving papyrus and fragment numbers, 'sequitur' ('there follows'), and the apparatus lines listing isolated legible words ('us.' = line) are rendered as such. 53.9 δόνταϲ read as δόνταϲ = δόνταϲ for δόνταϲ/δόνταϲ (likely δόντα〈ϲ〉, 'granting'). 63.10 ἐνθουϲιαϲτικαῖϲ ἐπιτάϲεϲιν: sense of the construction unclear as the sentence breaks off. 68.2–5: 'they renamed' (μετωνόμαϲαν) placed by sense; the subject and object are lost.

Most of this stretch consists of tiny, mutilated fragments; only isolated words could be rendered, and many lines are untranslatable sequences of letters (given as '. . .'). Editorial lines in Latin (fragment numbers, descriptions, 'us.' = lines) are rendered in English. 77.12 ἰδ[ίᾳ ('of itself') is uncertain. 78.2 'pap. 434' conflicts with the heading's 424; the edition's error is kept. 78.26 Κλεαν- is taken as Cleanthes. 4.1B.4: the restoration εὐϲχήμονοϲ ('decent') seems to contradict φορτικῆϲ; 'indecent' (ἀϲχήμονοϲ) is adopted as the likely sense. 73.7 '(sic)' marks the edition's own query on γεγόναϲιν.

Heavily damaged columns; many restorations are Kemke's. 4.2.30–36: the identity of the 'more natural-minded' group and the object of 'declaring spurious' (νοθίζοντες) is uncertain. 4.4.14 '(ου-' read as μου-. 4.5.1–5: wordplay deriving θεωρεῖν, θεατής, θέατρον from θεῖν 'run' rather than θεῖον 'divine'. 4.5.32 ἀπαρχὴ τοῦ γένους: sense uncertain ('first-offering for the family/offspring'). 4.6.12–13 the supplement 'they cease' is conjectural; 4.6.25 lacuna.

Text is heavily lacunose; many restorations are Kemke's. 'Diogenes' is presumably Diogenes of Babylon, the Stoic opponent. 4.7.10–11: sense of 'for the most part composed' for women is uncertain. 4.8.15 'those who haul down' (καθέλκουσιν) likely refers to launching or hauling ships; the Ptolemy meant is unidentified (probably a Ptolemaic king). 4.8.18–20 construed as 'when the musicians stop, the workers no longer accomplish'; uncertain. 4.9.29–30 καθέλκονγων, ϲώμαγα read as καθελκόντων, σώματα. 4.10.2 Crexus: a dithyrambic poet, poem unidentified. 4.10.20–21 the 'honour' clause is uncertain. 4.11.19, 4.11.29 partly illegible.

The papyrus is heavily damaged throughout; much of the text rests on Kemke's restorations, and many lines are fragmentary. In 12.1 βαρβ[...] cannot be restored securely. In 16.31-32 the sense of 'not their own' (αὐτῶν) is inferred. The closing lines (17.8-11) are uncertain; the construction of 'not [calling] Homer...' depends on the following lines. 'Persaeus' (14.13) is presumably the Stoic Persaeus of Citium.

The text is heavily restored and in places obscure. 17.12–16: the sense of 'colours' and the construction are uncertain. 18.34–36: 'τοῖϲ ἀδιανοήτοιϲ' may mean the Spartans are 'witless' witnesses or witnesses to 'unthinkable' things. 19.4 'Πέρπανδρον' is read as Terpander. 21.16 'ἀφετεουϲ' is read as ἀφετέουϲ, 'to be dismissed', which is uncertain. 21.29–30 and 21.39 are lacunose. 'Diogenes' here is presumably Diogenes of Babylon.

Line 22.1: the opening letters εαν are the end of a lost word. Line 22.5: τὴν ἀπὸ φρονήσεως is elliptical; the noun understood (devotion, or benefit) is uncertain. Line 22.23: the edition's ἢ[ε] is doubtful; read as ἤ 'or'. Line 22.36: ἀνταποδιδόναι τὸ μέλος, 'rendering back the melody', may refer to performing or reproducing a melody; the sense is uncertain. Line 22.39: φρονε[...] is broken off; it may be a form of φρονεῖν or φρόνησις.

Line 4.23.1: the referent of αὐτῷ is lost in the preceding gap. The Diogenes sentence (4.23.27 onward) is grammatically incomplete; its main verb presumably followed the clause ending at 4.24.9, so the English is somewhat restructured across 4.24.4–9. 4.24.22: ἐ|λ]άλουν is read as ἐλάλουν, 'chattered'. 4.24.39–41 are largely lost: only 'of the craftsmen' and a form of πλεονεκ- ('overreach') can be read.

Col. 25.5–6: 'as are lawsuits, sights' is obscure; the text may be corrupt. Col. 25.27: lacuna after 'through the'; the word is unrestored. Col. 25.36–40: too fragmentary for connected sense. Col. 26.15: 'boorish' rests on the restoration ἀγροικευόμεθα. Col. 26.37: 'conclusion' renders ἐπιφορά; the sense is uncertain.

Text heavily damaged; lines 27.27–27.30 and 27.38–27.40 largely illegible and translated only in fragments. Supplements such as [φωνῶ]ν at 28.29 and [παιδ]ευόντων at 27.21 are the editor's, some marked doubtful. In 28.5–9 'bare' (ψιλοῦ) likely means 'unadorned [prose]'.

Column 30 is badly damaged in lines 1–7 and 25–26; only fragments are translated. Lines 4.29.16–17 are garbled in the edition (a supplement 〈καλεῖν μουϲικούϲ〉 is inserted); the sense seems to be that Aristoxenus, nicknamed 'the musician', calls instrumental composers musicians. In 4.29.23 the '26' is a stray line number. 'ἱλαρωκέναι' (29.29) is a supplement. Line 4.30.27 is not text but the edition's critical apparatus (variant readings or supplements keyed to line numbers), rendered as such.

Text heavily damaged throughout; many restorations are the editor's and some are marked doubtful. 4.31.22 is the edition's apparatus of readings for lines 26–29, not continuous text. 4.32.16: 'ὑποκρινομένου[ου' shows a doubled syllable, read as ὑποκρινομένου. 4.32.31–33: μειμητικάϲ = μιμητικάϲ; μι[ι]μ- = μιμ-; 'music-like' renders the restored μουϲικῇ παραπληϲίοιϲ ('similar to music'). The construction of 4.32.30–39 is uncertain.

33.6: καταϲτήϲει ('will render') completes the clause of 33.1–5. 33.36–37: lacuna; the verb of the second 'many' clause is lost and has been supplied conjecturally. 34.10: π[λὰ] read as πολλὰ. 34.15–16: the subject of 'promoted' (προήγαγον) is unstated, presumably the Athenians and Greeks. 34.39: 'δύο λαβεῖν' ('to take two') does not construe clearly here; the text is probably corrupt or wrongly restored, and the line is left untranslated in part.

The text is lacunose at 4.35.40–42; only isolated words survive there. At 4.36.20–23 the restorations τὰϲ, τἆλλα and ἔργον are queried in the edition, so the sense of that sentence is uncertain. At 4.35.13–17 the reference of 'the two [points] before it' and 'the last' depends on lost preceding argument.

The papyrus is fragmentary; restorations follow the edition's brackets. Line 37 'ἀπρέπειαν' is marked doubtful in the edition. Lines 6–7 (τὰ δύϲγνωϲτα μὲν ἁπάντων ὅϲῳ ϲυμφορώτερα) are syntactically uncertain; the rendering is tentative. Line 8 has a stray period after καὶ, omitted. The sentence at line 40 continues into the next stretch and its sense is incomplete.

The text is badly damaged throughout. Line 1 begins with a lost word ending in -μαϲιν. In lines 23–25 the construction (ἢ ... ἀφίϲτηϲι) is incomplete, perhaps owing to a lost alternative; the sense is uncertain. Lines 41–42 are largely illegible; θαυμάϲια and πεπιϲτευκότων are restorations.

Plato, Laws II 669B: 'For since it is celebrated more than the other images, it needs the greatest caution of all images. For whoever errs in it would be harmed most gravely, welcoming bad characters; and it is very hard to perceive, because the poets are inferior to the Muses themselves. For they would never err so far as to give men's words a women's figure and melody, or, having composed the melody and figures of free men, to fit rhythms of slaves and unfree men to them; nor again, having laid down free rhythms and figure, to give a melody or words contrary to the rhythms; nor would they ever put together in one the cries of beasts and of men and of instruments and all sorts of sounds, as if imitating one thing. But human poets, heavily interweaving and jumbling such things together irrationally, would provide laughter for all those men who, as Orpheus says, have come to the season of delight. For they see all these things jumbled together; and the poets further tear apart rhythm and figures from melody, setting bare words into metres, and melody and rhythm without words, using bare lyre-playing and pipe-playing, in which it is very hard to recognise, when rhythm and harmony arise without words, what they mean and which of the worthy imitations they resemble. One must rather assume that everything of this sort is full of much boorishness, insofar as it is very fond of speed and unfaltering dexterity and bestial sound, so as to use pipe-playing and lyre-playing other than to accompany dance and song; and the use of either bare would be utterly unmusical showmanship.'

Plato, Laws 802B: 'Those chosen as examiners of these, not younger than fifty years, are to make the selection: whatever of the old poems seems adequate they are to admit; whatever is deficient or wholly unsuitable, the one they are to reject altogether, the other to take up again and rework, enlisting men skilled in poetry and music, using their powers of composition, but not yielding to their pleasures and desires except in a few cases, and expounding the wishes of the lawgiver, so as to arrange dance and song and all choral performance as far as possible according to their own judgement. Every disorderly pursuit concerning music, once it takes on order, even without the sweet Muse being set beside it, is ten thousand times better; the pleasant is common to all. For if someone lives from childhood to the settled and sensible age in temperate and ordered music, hearing the opposite he hates it and calls it unfree; but if raised in the common and sweet sort, he says its opposite is cold and unpleasant.'
